lesson.title: The Rules of the Line: Scheduling Disciplines Beyond Fair Queuing
lesson.summary: A scheduling discipline is the general rule a router uses to decide which queued packet a shared outbound link transmits next; fair queuing is one important example, but FIFO and priority-based disciplines each make a very different trade-off.
lesson.body:
Fair queuing, covered in the previous chapter, is one specific answer to a more general question. Whenever multiple packets are sitting in a router waiting for the same outbound link, some rule has to decide the order they leave in. That rule, whatever it happens to be, is called a scheduling discipline. It is worth naming the whole category, not just fair queuing, because the right choice depends entirely on what an operator is actually trying to optimize, and fairness is only one of several possible goals.

A short survey shows the range of trade-offs available. First-in-first-out is the simplest option and the historical default: packets leave in the exact order they arrived, with no separation between flows at all, which is precisely the lack of isolation that motivated fair queuing in the first place. Strict priority queuing keeps multiple queues ranked by importance and always fully drains a higher-priority queue before serving a lower-priority one at all. This gives excellent, almost unconditional guarantees to whatever sits in the top queue, for example voice traffic, but it comes with a real risk: if the high-priority queue is never empty, the lower-priority queues can be starved indefinitely, receiving no service whatsoever. Round robin and fair queuing, covered previously, sit between these two extremes, giving every flow a guaranteed minimum share by taking turns, at the cost of more bookkeeping and per-flow state than FIFO needs. Weighted fair queuing and its many practical descendants, such as deficit round robin, which exists because true bit-by-bit weighted fair queuing cannot actually run at full line rate in hardware, generalize round robin further so that different classes receive proportional shares rather than strictly identical ones.

This matters practically because a router or switch's configured scheduling discipline is exactly where the abstract prioritization goal from the QoS chapter gets enforced, one packet at a time, at every hop along a path. DiffServ, covered two chapters ahead, tells a router which class a given packet belongs to by marking it, but it is the local scheduling discipline actually running on that router's outbound interface that decides, in real time, when a packet carrying that mark actually gets to leave.

Running the same three-flow scenario from the fair queuing chapter through strict priority instead of round robin makes the difference sharp. If flow A is marked high priority and flows B and C are both low priority, A is served ahead of B and C in every single round it has anything queued, even if that means B and C wait indefinitely whenever A is active. That is a fundamentally different outcome from fair queuing's guaranteed minimum share for every flow, and neither discipline is simply better, they are appropriate for different goals: fair queuing when every flow deserves a floor, strict priority when one class's needs genuinely outrank everything else's.
